faq.a: Yes, co‑infection is common, especially in HIV‑positive children; each virus may produce its own clinical picture.
faq.q: Can a child be infected with more than one HHV at once?

faq.a: CMV lacks the viral kinase that activates acyclovir; ganciclovir is required for DNA chain termination.
faq.q: Why is acyclovir ineffective against CMV?

faq.a: A varicella vaccine exists and is increasingly used in low‑resource settings; no vaccine is available for HSV, CMV, EBV or HHV‑8.
faq.q: Is there a vaccine for any HHV?

exam: A 10‑month‑old presents with high fever for 4 days then a maculopapular rash that spares the trunk – what is the most likely virus and why? — HHV‑6 roseola; fever precedes rash due to viral replication then abrupt immune clearance.

A child with known HIV develops violaceous nodules on the palate – which virus is responsible and what systemic therapy improves survival? — HHV‑8 Kaposi sarcoma; start HAART to restore immunity, consider liposomal doxorubicin if lesions threaten airway.

A newborn has petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly and sensorineural hearing loss – which test confirms the diagnosis and what does a positive IgM indicate? — CMV PCR or IgM serology; IgM shows recent congenital infection.

A 5‑year‑old with severe malnutrition has vesicular lesions on the lips and a painful ulcer on the tongue – which virus and what first‑line drug should you give? — HHV‑1 (herpes gingivostomatitis); give oral acyclovir, avoiding nephrotoxic drugs if renal function unknown.

A child on chemotherapy develops fever, cough and diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest X‑ray – which HHV should you suspect and what is the preferred antiviral? — CMV pneumonitis; give ganciclovir, monitoring blood counts.

During a malaria outbreak, a child presents with fever, splenomegaly and a faint maculopapular rash – how do you differentiate HHV‑6 roseola from malaria? — Roseola rash appears after fever resolves; malaria shows persistent fever and positive rapid test.

A teenager with recurrent genital ulcers tests negative for HSV PCR – what other HHV should be considered and why? — HHV‑2 (genital HSV) is most common, but HHV‑8 can cause ulcerative lesions in immunocompromised patients; consider HIV testing.

In a resource‑limited ward, you suspect VZV encephalitis but lack PCR – what clinical clues guide treatment and what drug do you start? — Altered mental status with vesicular rash; start high‑dose acyclovir empirically.
ai.title: Human Herpesviruses
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Human herpesviruses (HHV‑1 to HHV‑8) cause common childhood infections and serious disease in immunocompromised children. Understanding transmission, clinical patterns and limited diagnostics in low‑resource settings guides timely management.

b: Eight species (HHV‑1 to HHV‑8)
Latency in sensory ganglia, monocytes or endothelial cells
Reactivation triggered by stress, illness or immunosuppression
sections.p: Human herpesviruses are DNA viruses that establish lifelong latency after primary infection. In children they range from benign exanthems to life‑threatening organ disease, especially when HIV or malnutrition is present.

b: γ‑herpesviruses (HHV‑4, HHV‑8) have strong oncogenic potential
α‑herpesviruses (HHV‑1, HHV‑2) cause rapid lytic disease
sections.p: All HHVs are enveloped double‑stranded DNA viruses. They share a lytic phase (viral replication, cell death) and a latent phase (minimal gene expression, no virion production).

b: Close contact in day‑care spreads HHV‑1 (cold sores) and HHV‑6 (roseola)
Maternal CMV infection is a leading cause of congenital sensorineural hearing loss
sections.p: Transmission varies: saliva (HHV‑1, HHV‑6), sexual contact (HHV‑8), blood/organ transplant (CMV, HHV‑8), and vertical (CMV). After entry the virus replicates locally, spreads to regional ganglia or bone‑marrow, and then establishes latency.

b: HHV‑1: gingivostomatitis, encephalitis (rare)
HHV‑2: genital ulcer disease, neonatal infection
VZV (HHV‑3): varicella, herpes zoster, cerebellar ataxia
EBV (HHV‑4): infectious mononucleosis, endemic Burkitt lymphoma
CMV (HHV‑5): congenital infection, retinitis in HIV, colitis
HHV‑6/7: roseola infantum, febrile seizures
HHV‑8: Kaposi sarcoma, especially in HIV‑positive children
sections.p: Clinical syndromes depend on the virus, host age and immune status. In low‑resource settings, co‑infection with HIV, malaria or malnutrition worsens outcomes.
In many African hospitals, definitive virology is limited. Diagnosis relies on clinical patterns, basic labs and selective use of rapid tests.

t.b: Detects multinucleated giant cells – suggests a herpesvirus but cannot differentiate species
IgM positive indicates recent infection; if unavailable, consider congenital CMV if newborn has petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, or sensorineural hearing loss

t.a: PCR on blood or CSF (if available)
t.b: Confirms viral DNA; when unavailable, treat empirically based on syndrome

b: Acyclovir (HSV, VZV) – first‑line; avoid if renal function unknown
Ganciclovir/valganciclovir (CMV) – reserved for severe disease; monitor marrow toxicity
No specific drug for HHV‑6/7 – treat fever and seizures symptomatically
HAART for HIV reduces HHV‑8‑related Kaposi sarcoma
sections.p: Therapy focuses on antiviral agents when available, supportive care, and prevention of reactivation in high‑risk children.

t.a: Baseline CBC and renal function before acyclovir
t.b: Ensures safe dosing; if labs unavailable, use lowest effective dose and monitor urine output
Detects keratitis early; if ophthalmology not available, refer urgently

b: Cold sores + fever in a toddler → HHV‑1 gingivostomatitis
High fever > 3 days then sudden rash → HHV‑6 roseola
Congenital sensorineural hearing loss + periventricular calcifications → CMV
Violaceous skin lesions in HIV child → HHV‑8 Kaposi sarcoma
sections.p: Think of HHV when a child presents with a vesicular rash, fever with a characteristic exanthem, or unexplained organ disease in an immunocompromised host.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe respiratory distress from VZV pneumonia
Unexplained severe anemia or thrombocytopenia in CMV infection
Progressive Kaposi sarcoma compromising airway or bleeding
